passages.provision_quote: I think in the case of California we'll need new revenue and there are people who aren't paying their fair share who have to pay a little bit more.
passages.note: Campaign interview: new revenue from wealthy investment-income holders, paired with program cuts to balance the books; shows the raise-taxes side, purpose and size not tied to one rung.

passages.provision_quote: So principally it would be looking at some of the passive income, some of the investment income where, which is where so many wealthy individuals make so much money and pay very low tax rates for that investment income.
passages.note: Would raise taxes on wealthy investment income and would raise revenue to fund Prop 36 services; no magnitude, and the funded services point toward new spending while other passages point to existing budget needs.

passages.provision_quote: That, by implication, means that billionaires who pay at a tax rate lower than a teacher are going to pay more in taxes.
passages.note: Opposes the one-time billionaire tax but wants billionaires to pay more and backs reauthorizing Prop 30/55; side is clear, size and purpose (new vs existing services) are not.

passages.provision_quote: But no doubt, billionaires in California, too many of them are not paying their fair share.
passages.note: General-election debate: votes no on the billionaire tax initiative, opposes broad tax cuts, says billionaires underpay; direction only.

passages.provision_quote: in fact he actually calls for getting rid of some of the corporate welfare loopholes that are allowing corporations to pay less
passages.note: Would change the tax code so billionaires do not pay lower rates than workers and cites closing corporate loopholes; mixes a rate-raising aim with a rung-3 loophole clause.
'Everyone should pay their fair share' with no policy clause.
Film tax credit expansion is an industry incentive, not the tax-versus-services balance the rungs order.

rows.reasoning: His own campaign words consistently call for wealthy people, especially those with investment income, to pay more ('there are people who aren't paying their fair share who have to pay a little bit more'), which places him on the raise-taxes side of the ladder. They do not separate 'significantly raise taxes ... to fund more public services' from 'moderately raise taxes ... to fund existing services': he pairs new revenue with balancing the budget and cuts in one passage, but would raise revenue to fund Prop 36 services in another, and he also cites closing corporate loopholes.

quotes.text: So principally it would be looking at some of the passive income, some of the investment income where, which is where so many wealthy individuals make so much money and pay very low tax rates for that investment income.
